scenario.name: Peer help marketplace
scenario.idea: A student-to-student marketplace where AI matches helpers to requests and payments go through the app.

advisor.summary: This marketplace handles location, messages and payment data for students who may be minors, so child privacy, user safety and payment handling are the most urgent areas to check before launch. Bias in AI matching, third-party API data flows and misleading-claims exposure also need mitigation as you grow.

risks.severityWhy: Minors' data (location, messages, payment info) is collected and no safeguard is described.
risks.title: Children's and minors' data collection
risks.why: Users may include children under 13 and other minors. You collect precise location, private messages and payment info. Children's privacy rules MAY apply, including parental consent expectations. Whether they apply depends on your actual age range, which you did not state.
risks.fix: Set and enforce a minimum age with an age gate. Collect location only at coarse level (campus or area) and only when needed. Set short retention periods for messages and location history. Add a parental consent flow if under-13 users are possible. Block under-13 sign-up if you can't support that.

risks.severityWhy: Direct harm to people is possible: minors may be connected with strangers, with no safeguard described.
risks.title: Minor safety in matching, messaging and meetups
risks.why: The AI matches students with helpers, and messages and location are shared. That could expose minors to adult impersonators, grooming, harassment or in-person risk. No listed source directly addresses this risk, so it needs review by a professional.
risks.fix: Verify users (for example school email) and separate minors from adults. Keep communication in-app only, with no sharing of exact location or contact details. Add report and block buttons, message screening for risky content, and a human moderation queue. Default to public, supervised meeting spots or remote help.

risks.severityWhy: Could block launch: money flows between users through the app, and minors may be involved.
risks.title: Holding or moving user money
risks.why: If your app receives, holds or transfers funds between students, money transmission rules MAY apply to you at federal and state level. Whether they do depends on how the payment flow is structured, which you did not describe. Minors' ability to contract and pay adds more questions.
risks.fix: Use a licensed payment processor or marketplace payments product so that funds are never held in your own account. Document the flow of funds. Require a parent or guardian account for minors. Add refund and dispute handling.

risks.severityWhy: Sensitive data (payment info, minors' location and messages) is held and no safeguards are described.
risks.title: Data security and breach readiness
risks.why: A breach could expose minors' locations, private messages and payment details. NC's breach notification law MAY apply when you hold residents' personal information.
risks.fix: Never store raw card data; use tokenized payments. Encrypt data in transit and at rest. Apply role-based access controls and audit logs, and delete data on a schedule. Write an incident response plan that names who decides on and sends notifications.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: user messages and data may be sent to a third-party API, and mitigation is needed before scaling.
risks.title: Student data sent to a third-party AI API
risks.why: Sending messages, location or profile data to an outside model provider can leak minors' data. It may also be retained or used for training. Models can also produce made-up output, or be manipulated through prompt injection in messages. What you send to the API was not specified.
risks.fix: Send only the minimum fields needed for matching (such as subject, skill and availability tags) and never raw messages, exact location or payment data. Strip identifiers before API calls. Get a no-training, minimal-retention contract with the provider. Treat user text as untrusted input and validate model outputs.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: matching steers earning opportunities among people, though a human remains in the loop; this needs mitigation before scaling.
risks.title: Unequal matching of helpers and requests
risks.why: AI matching could favor some helpers or requesters based on proxies such as school, location, name, writing style or ratings history. That could disadvantage groups of students in who gets paid work or help. Because a human only gets informed, they may rubber-stamp AI suggestions.
risks.fix: Exclude sensitive attributes and obvious proxies from matching inputs. Regularly compare match and earnings rates across user groups and locations. Give new helpers a fair-exposure rule. Let users choose or override matches, and keep a way to appeal or report unfair treatment.

risks.severityWhy: Plausibly applies: safety, AI and fee claims could be misleading, and this needs mitigation before wider release.
risks.title: Misleading claims about safety, AI or fees
risks.why: Unfair and deceptive practice rules MAY apply if you overstate how safe, vetted or accurate the matching is, hide fees, or don't make clear that AI is involved. Claims aimed at minors and parents may get closer scrutiny.
risks.fix: Review all marketing, in-app copy and safety claims against what you actually do. Disclose that AI does the matching and what data it uses. Show fees and refund terms before payment. Keep evidence for every safety or quality claim.

askLawyer: Given that our users may include minors, what age-gating, parental consent and contract rules should we plan for, and does COPPA or any NC student privacy law apply to us if schools get involved?
Does our payment flow make us a money transmitter, or can a licensed processor keep us out of that category, and how should payments by minors be handled?
What breach notification, retention and vendor-contract terms should we put in place for minors' location, messages and payment data shared with a third-party AI provider?

plain.text:
# Risk Assessment: Student Marketplace with AI Matching

## Highest-severity risks

### 1. Child safety
- **Adult impersonation and grooming.** Without strong verification, adults can pose as students and target minors. Matching people by proximity, plus private messaging, is the classic risk pattern.
- **In-person meetings.** Tutoring, errands, or other help can put minors alone with strangers, including older students or adults.
- **Location exposure.** Precise location data on minors is both a safety hazard and a regulatory flashpoint.
- **Harassment, bullying, and coercion** in messages, including pressure around payment.

**Mitigations:**
- Verify students (school email, or school-partnered onboarding) and check age.
- Separate minors from adults, or restrict to same-school or same-age bands.
- Use coarse location only (school or zone, not GPS).
- Keep messaging in-app with moderation, reporting, and blocking.
- Default to public meeting places or virtual sessions.
- Set up an escalation path for safety incidents.

### 2. Children's privacy and data law
- **COPPA** applies if any users are under 13, and it requires verifiable parental consent. The FTC has also tightened its rule on third-party data sharing and retention. Even if you target 13+, you need an age gate that works.
- **FTC Act Section 5** covers unfair or deceptive practices, including sloppy handling of teen data.
- **FERPA** may apply if you integrate with schools or receive school records.
- **North Carolina law** includes breach notification and identity theft statutes. Check current NC developments, and note that if you have users in other states, those states' privacy and minor-protection laws (such as age-appropriate design and social media laws) may apply.
- Messages, location, and payment data together form a high-sensitivity profile of a minor.

**Mitigations:** Data minimization, short retention periods, clear parental consent flows where needed, a privacy policy written for teens, and a legal review before launch.

### 3. Payments involving minors
- **Contract capacity.** Minors can generally void contracts, which creates refund and dispute exposure.
- **Money transmission rules.** Holding and moving funds between users may trigger licensing requirements unless you use a licensed processor's marketplace product (e.g., Stripe Connect) and structure it carefully.
- **KYC and AML.** Payout accounts generally require adult or verified identities, so minors may need custodial accounts.
- **Fraud.** Scams, stolen cards, chargebacks, and off-platform payment steering.
- **Tax reporting** for earners (1099-K thresholds).
- **PCI scope.** Never store card data yourself.

### 4. Child labor and work classification
- Paid help from minors can implicate the **NC Youth Employment Act** and federal FLSA rules, including age limits, hours, and prohibited tasks. Depending on the services, it may also raise independent contractor classification questions.
- Restrict the allowed service categories (e.g., no driving, childcare, heavy labor, or anything hazardous).

## Medium-severity risks

### 5. Third-party AI API
- **Data flow to the vendor.** Sending minors' messages or location to an external model raises consent, retention, and COPPA/FTC concerns. Confirm zero-retention terms, no training on your data, and a data processing agreement.
- **Prompt injection and manipulation.** Users could craft profiles or messages that game matching or extract other users' data.
- **Vendor dependency.** Outages, pricing changes, model updates that silently change matching behavior, and policy changes.
- **Minimize inputs.** Send pseudonymized, minimal features rather than raw messages or exact locations wherever possible.

### 6. AI matching quality and fairness
- **Bias.** Matching or ranking can disadvantage people by race, gender, disability, income, school, or language. This can mean unequal access to earning opportunities.
- **Unsafe matches.** The AI might pair a minor with a mismatched helper, such as a much older one or someone with prior reports, if safety signals aren't hard constraints.
- **Automation bias.** "Informs a human" only helps if the human can actually evaluate and override the match. Students may just accept the top suggestion.
- **Opacity.** Users should be able to see why they were matched and to opt out.

**Mitigations:** Hard-coded safety rules that sit outside the model, bias audits, explanations for matches, and feedback loops.

### 7. Content moderation
- Messages may include harassment, sexual content, self-harm disclosures, drug sales, or off-platform contact solicitation.
- LLM-based moderation has false negatives and false positives, so combine it with rules, human review, and clear reporting channels.
- Consider mandatory reporting obligations and NCMEC reporting duties if you encounter CSAM.

### 8. Academic integrity
- If helpers can sell essays, homework, or exam help, you risk schools banning the app, reputational damage, and possible legal exposure under contract cheating laws. Define permitted services (tutoring and feedback versus completing assignments).

## Other risks

- **Platform liability.** Section 230 offers limited protection against claims about your own design choices, such as negligent matching or inadequate safety features. Expect scrutiny from parents, schools, and regulators.
- **Security.** A breach exposing minors' locations, messages, and payment info would be severe. Use encryption, access controls, and logging.
- **App store policies.** Apple and Google have strict rules for apps aimed at minors, user-generated content, and payments.
- **Trust and adoption.** Schools and parents may resist unless safety is visible and credible.
- **Disputes.** You need processes for no-shows, poor service, refunds, and false accusations.

## Suggested first steps
1. Decide on the age range. Restricting to 13+ or 16+, or to verified college students, dramatically reduces legal complexity.
2. Choose a licensed payments platform and define allowed service types.
3. Design safety-by-default: verified identities, coarse location, in-app messaging, and public or virtual sessions.
4. Draft a data map covering what goes to the AI vendor, along with a vendor agreement.
5. Run a privacy and safety review with counsel experienced in children's privacy and fintech.
6. Pilot with a single school or campus partner before opening it up.

*This is a general risk overview, not legal advice. Because of the minors and payments combination, consult an attorney before launch.*
